clue.text: Keep some wood behind this place - officially

indicators.note: behind puts the wood after the place in the answer, though the clue names the wood first

blocks.note: a keep is the stronghold of a castle
the place where the speaker is
a cord is a measured stack of cut firewood

explanation.surface: Someone is asked to keep a supply of timber stacked behind the building, and wants it on the official record.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Behind' places the wood after this place, so the timber follows HERE; a cord is a standard volume of firewood, 128 cubic feet.
explanation.definitionFit: Something said on the record is said formally, so it is stated publicly and in an official capacity.

clue.text: Insectivore flourished — person's upset

indicators.note: upset means turned upside down, and in a down answer that flips the order

blocks.note: fl. stands for floruit, Latin for flourished, used of dates
a party is a person, as in a third party

explanation.surface: A bug-eater was thriving until someone disturbed it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Person's' is person is: the person is turned over. FL is the scholars' abbreviation for floruit, flourished.
explanation.definitionFit: The Venus fly-trap is a carnivorous plant that catches and digests insects, so it is an insect-eater.

clue.text: About to ruin one line, acquire new lines

blocks.note: re means about, concerning
to mar is to spoil
Ry is short for railway, a single railway line

explanation.surface: Someone about to wreck a railway line takes on new ones.
explanation.walkthrough: Marriage lines are a British name for a marriage certificate, so acquiring new lines means a fresh wedding.
explanation.definitionFit: To remarry is to wed again, getting a new marriage certificate, the document traditionally called marriage lines.

clue.text: Well may bear examination

blocks.note: surface reading: a good deep well is expected to stay full
setter's reading: an argument that stands up to scrutiny is sound

explanation.walkthrough: 'Well' looks like the adverb, as in 'well may you ask', but it is the hole for drawing water, which the phrase literally describes.
explanation.definitionFit: An argument or theory that holds water is sound and convincing, standing up to close scrutiny.

clue.text: Man who's received everywhere

blocks.note: first meaning: a man's name
second meaning: the radio word for message received, understood in every country

explanation.surface: A popular man is welcomed wherever he goes.
explanation.definitionFit: In radio procedure 'Roger' is the standard reply confirming a message has been heard and understood.

clue.text: Nazi car crashed by empress

indicators.note: a crashed car is smashed out of shape, so the letters are wrecked and reordered

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A German staff car is driven into by a Russian empress.
explanation.definitionFit: A czarina was the wife of a czar or a Russian empress ruling in her own right.

clue.text: Painter beginning to paint girl — rising artist

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter
in a down answer, rising means reading upwards, so the name runs backwards

blocks.note: RA is a Royal Academician, a recognised artist
only the opening letter is kept
a girl's name

explanation.surface: A young woman starts painting and becomes an up-and-coming artist.
explanation.walkthrough: RA, a member of the Royal Academy of Arts in London, is the crossword's stock artist; it goes first though it is last in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Raphael was a master painter of the Italian High Renaissance, famed for his Madonnas and Vatican frescoes.

clue.text: Lines missing, following. . .

indicators.note: following puts the word for missing after what comes next in the run-on clue

blocks.note: the dots carry the clue on into the next one, whose hereafter is heaven
a plain synonym

explanation.surface: Some lines of text are absent from what comes next.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links this clue to 10 down: its 'hereafter' supplies the heavenly half here, and 'following' puts missing after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Paradise Lost is Milton's epic poem, and lines are verse, so the poem is a body of lines.

clue.text: Little by little, not extremely profound

indicators.note: not to the extreme means stopping short of the far end, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: a as in 'a little': the article standing for a small amount
taken as written
a plain synonym

explanation.surface: Something is done gradually, bit by bit, but never goes very deep.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase 'little by little' looks like an idiom for gradually, but it splits into three pieces; the first 'Little' supplying only A is a loose stretch by the setter.
explanation.definitionFit: Abysmal literally means as deep as an abyss, so it can describe profound depths, as in abysmal ignorance.

clue.text: Come to grips with Greek fruit

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation
an example of fruit

explanation.surface: Someone tackles a Greek fruit, perhaps a pomegranate that is hard to open.
explanation.definitionFit: To grapple is to seize and wrestle with an opponent or a problem, taking hold of it firmly.

clue.text: . . . hereafter, call for a love-token

blocks.note: the life after death
to ring is to telephone

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: an appeal for a keepsake to last into the afterlife.
explanation.definitionFit: An eternity ring, set with stones all round its band, is a gift symbolising lasting love between partners.

clue.text: Plainsmen, so to speak, boasted on the radio

indicators.note: in an across answer, one thing on another sits after it, so the first word follows the second

blocks.note: broadcasting is being on the air
an old past tense of crow, to brag

explanation.surface: Men from the prairies brag about themselves in a radio broadcast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plainsmen' looks like prairie dwellers; 'so to speak' warns it is a pun on planes-men, the people who fly an aircraft.
explanation.definitionFit: An aircrew is the team who operate an aeroplane, so they are men of the plane by a punning spelling.

clue.text: Surrey town — agree with it being developed

indicators.note: something being developed is being reshaped and rebuilt, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A planning dispute: a Surrey town consents to building work going ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: Surrey is a county just south of London; REIGATE is one of its market towns.
explanation.definitionFit: Reigate is a commuter town in the English county of Surrey, so it is named by its location.

clue.text: Just wanting a second hint

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so the word is missing something

blocks.note: just as in 'it's just wrong'
s is the abbreviation for second

explanation.surface: Someone only needs one more clue to get the answer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Just' looks like an adjective for fair, but it is the adverb meaning merely; take S away from the front.
explanation.definitionFit: To imply is to suggest something without saying it outright, which is what hinting does.

clue.text: Jack, a man wearing waterproof hat

blocks.note: Jack tar is a sailor, and a tar is a sailor
any man's name will do
dressed in

explanation.surface: A sailor called Jack puts on a hat that keeps the rain off.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pairs Jack and the hat as one sailor in sou'wester; in the wordplay 'wearing' is just IN tacked on the end, not a container.
explanation.definitionFit: A tarpaulin was a sailor's tarred, rainproof hat, named after the tarred canvas it was made from.

clue.text: Wrongdoer trained to be a porter

indicators.note: trained means shaped and drilled into a new form, so the letters take a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A criminal is given training to work as a porter, rehabilitation through honest work.
explanation.definitionFit: A reprobate is an unprincipled, immoral person, a scoundrel who habitually behaves badly.

clue.text: Adverse winds leading operator to listen in

indicators.note: to wind is to twist and turn, so the letters are twisted into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
op is short for an operator, as in radio op

explanation.surface: Contrary winds direct a radio operator to tune in and listen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Winds' reads as weather but is a verb; the rearranged word leads, coming before the operator.
explanation.definitionFit: To eavesdrop is to secretly overhear a private conversation, which is listening in on it.

clue.text: Savage born in the purple

indicators.note: in puts one piece inside the other

blocks.note: n. abbreviates natus, Latin for born, in genealogies
violet is a purple colour

explanation.surface: A cruel tyrant was of royal birth, born to the purple.
explanation.walkthrough: To be born in the purple is to be born into royalty; here the phrase splits into born, in and purple.
explanation.definitionFit: Violent and savage both describe fierce, brutal behaviour that uses physical force to harm.

clue.text: Southern ploughman is less ruffled

blocks.note: the abbreviation
one who tills the soil

explanation.surface: A farm worker from the south keeps calmer than others.
explanation.definitionFit: Still water is calm and unruffled, so something stiller is more placid, with fewer ripples on it.

clue.text: Often Etonians hold this opinion

indicators.note: the words hold the letters inside them, carried across the gap between the two

blocks.note: read straight through, ignoring the space

explanation.surface: Old Etonians, pupils of the famous school, often share a particular view.
explanation.walkthrough: Eton is England's best-known private school; its pupils are Etonians.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenet is a principle or belief held by a person or group, a firmly held opinion.

clue.text: Tuppence once accepted by doorkeeper for little fish

indicators.note: what is accepted is taken in, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: d was the old penny before decimal coinage, so two of them
a tiler, or tyler, guards the door of a Freemasons' lodge

explanation.surface: A doorman is tipped two pence in exchange for a tiny fish.
explanation.walkthrough: Before 1971 the British penny was written d, so tuppence was 2d. The Masonic doorkeeper is called the tiler.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiddler is an informal British word for a small fish such as a minnow or stickleback.

clue.text: Not a false note?

blocks.note: surface reading: something genuine, not put on
setter's reading: a musical note neither sharpened nor flattened

explanation.walkthrough: A false note sounds like a wrong note in music; the answer is both unaffected and a note that is neither sharp nor flat.
explanation.definitionFit: In music a natural is a note at its plain pitch, and natural also means genuine and unaffected.

clue.text: Dark blue, neat, being worn by Scotsman

blocks.note: neat is an old word for cattle, and an ox is one
clothes being worn are on
a typical Scottish name

explanation.surface: A smart navy outfit sits well on a Scotsman.
explanation.walkthrough: Oxford's colour is dark blue, Cambridge's light blue, so a Dark Blue is an Oxford man; neat here means cattle, not tidy.
explanation.definitionFit: Oxford University sportsmen are called Dark Blues after their colours, and an Oxonian is a member of that university.

clue.text: Mean to put up an animal shelter

indicators.note: in a down answer, putting something up means writing it bottom to top

blocks.note: taken as written
a sty is a pen for pigs

explanation.surface: Someone stingy intends to build a pen for livestock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put up' looks like build, and that is the surface; in the wordplay it turns the little word over.
explanation.definitionFit: Mean and nasty both describe unkind, spiteful behaviour toward other people.

clue.text: Senior Officer let down soldiers — they expect reliable leaders

indicators.note: the leaders of a line of words are the letters at the front of each one

blocks.clueFragment: Officer let down soldiers — they expect reliable
blocks.note: the opening letter of each of the seven words

explanation.surface: A senior officer has failed his troops, who expect to be able to trust their commanders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Senior Officer' reads as a rank, but the definition is Senior alone; the wordplay is the first letters of everything after it.
explanation.definitionFit: An oldster is an informal word for an older person, someone senior in years.

clue.text: A framework made of wooden strips — 18, possibly

definitions.text: A framework made of wooden strips

indicators.note: possibly means this is one way the letters could go, inviting another arrangement

blocks.note: the answer to 18 down

explanation.surface: A garden lattice of thin laths is described, perhaps for something calmer.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference points to the answer to 18 down, whose letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A trellis is a lattice of light crossed wooden laths, used to support climbing plants.

clue.text: Trouble gets Englishman in a flap

blocks.note: to ail is to trouble or afflict
E is the abbreviation for English
R is short for recipe, Latin for take
on as in 'on the team', a member of it

explanation.surface: An Englishman in a crisis gets into a panic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a flap' reads as panicking, but flap alone is the definition. 'Gets' is take, which a prescription abbreviates to R, and 'in' is ON as in 'the lights are on'.
explanation.definitionFit: An aileron is the hinged section on an aircraft's wing that tilts to bank the plane, a control flap.

clue.text: Dirty fuel, they say, is a cause of trouble

indicators.note: what people say is heard rather than read, so the spelling may differ

blocks.note: dirty weather is rough, stormy weather
petrol is the fuel for a car

explanation.surface: Contaminated petrol is blamed for causing engine trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: Petrol is the British word for gasoline. The seabird was thought to herald storms, hence its use for a troublemaker.
explanation.definitionFit: A stormy petrel is figuratively a person who brings trouble or delights in conflict, after the bird said to foretell storms.
